en: The *Sarvatathāgata-hṛdaya-rahasya-sarira-śarīra-ratna-peṭaka-mudrā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa of Daxingshan Monastery, Tejin, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Great Master of Vast Wisdom, Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying in the country of Magadha, within the Stainless Garden, at the Jewel Radiance Pond.
Together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great bodhisattvas, great śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
They surrounded him on all sides, front and back.
At that time, within the assembly, there was a great brahmin named Vimalaprabha (Stainless Wondrous Light), who was widely learned, wise, and a joy for all to behold;
he constantly practiced the ten wholesome paths and placed his faith and trust in the Triple Gem.
With a sincere and profound virtuous mind and subtle wisdom,
they constantly desire that all sentient beings may fulfill their wholesome benefits and attain great wealth and abundance.
Then the brahmin Vimalaprabha rose from his seat,
went to where the Buddha was, circumambulated the Buddha seven times,
and offered various fragrant flowers to the World-Honored One.
They covered the Buddha with priceless, exquisite robes, necklaces, and pearl garlands;
prostrating at his feet, they withdrew to stand to one side and made this request:
"We pray that the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly..."
"Come to my residence at dawn tomorrow to accept my offerings.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently granted his consent.
Then the brahmin knew that the Buddha had accepted his invitation.
He immediately returned to his residence and,
during the night, extensively prepared a hundred flavors of delicacies and food and drink;
he swept and cleansed the halls and pavilions, and unfurled banners and canopies.
When morning came, he, together with his retinue,
took various incenses, flowers, and musical instruments,
and went to where the Tathāgata was, saying, "The time has come."
"May you deign to descend.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke with gentle words to comfort the brahmin Vimalaprabha.
He addressed the great assembly, proclaiming:
"All of you should go to that brahmin's house to accept his offerings,
for the purpose of enabling him to obtain great benefit."
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat.
As soon as he had risen,
various kinds of light radiated forth from the Buddha’s body.
Interspersed with wondrous colors, they illuminated and touched the ten directions,
awakening them all before proceeding toward the Path.
At that time, the brahmin, with a mind of reverence, took exquisite incense and flowers.
Accompanied by his retinue and the eight classes of beings— devas, nāgas, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, together with Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings—
they first prepared the path and escorted the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One was not far ahead on the road.
He proceeded to a garden named Abhyudgata-śrī.
Within that garden stood an ancient, dilapidated stūpa, collapsed and ruined, its courtyard overgrown with thorns and its doors sealed by creeping weeds.
Burying it in rubble so that it resembled a mound of earth,
the World-Honored One then proceeded directly to the site of the stupa.
At that moment, the stupa emitted a great radiance, blazing with intense brilliance.
From within the heap of earth, a voice emerged, praising him and saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Śākyamuni!
What you have practiced today is a most sublime state."
Furthermore, O Brahmin, you have obtained great and wholesome benefit this very day.
At that time, the World-Honored One paid homage to that dilapidated stupa, circumambulated it three times to the right,
and removed his upper robe to cover it.
With tears streaming down his face, his blood mingled with his mucus;
having wept, he smiled.
At that moment, the Buddhas of the ten directions—
All gazed upon it together and likewise shed tears;
each emitted light that came to illuminate this stūpa.
At that time, the great assembly was struck with amazement and their complexions changed as they sought to resolve their mutual doubts.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others also shed tears;
with blazing and intense majesty, they brandished their vajras in a whirling motion and approached the Buddha, saying to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One..."
For what cause and condition does this manifestation of light appear?
Why do the eyes of the Tathāgata flow with tears in such a manner?
Furthermore, why do these great auspicious signs of light manifest before us from the Buddhas of the ten directions?
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain my doubts to this great assembly.
Then the Bhagavān addressed Vajrapāṇi:
"This is the precious stūpa of the Tathāgata, a mass of the entire body-relics."
The essential methods of the secret mudrās and dhāraṇīs of the immeasurable koṭis of hearts of all Tathāgatas are contained herein;
for it is because the Vajrapāṇi holds these essential methods within this [text].
The stūpa immediately transforms into a dense mass of layers without any gaps, like sesame seeds;
one should know that the bodies of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Tathāgatas are likewise like sesame seeds.
Within it is the collection of the entire bodily relics of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Tathāgatas;
even the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma are contained therein.
Furthermore, the cranial protuberances of nine hundred and ninety million koṭis of Tathāgatas are also contained therein.
Because of these wondrous qualities, wherever this stūpa is located,
there shall be great spiritual efficacy and extraordinary majesty,
capable of fulfilling all auspicious blessings for the world.
At that time, when the great assembly heard this teaching of the Buddha, they were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, severing all afflictions and attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.

Because the capacities of those in the assembly differed, their benefits were likewise distinct: [some attained] the fruit of a Srotāpanna, the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an Anāgāmin, the fruit of an Arhat, or the path of a Pratyekabuddha.
As well as the path of the bodhisattva, the state of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), and the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Regarding such matters, each attains one of these;
some may realize the first stage (*bhūmi*), the second stage, or even up to the tenth stage.
Some had fulfilled the six pāramitās;
that brahmin, having distanced himself from and departed from dust and defilement, attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
At that time, Vajrapāṇi beheld this extraordinary and rare event.
He addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "How wonderful and marvelous, World-Honored One!
If merely hearing of this matter brings such supreme merit, how much more merit would one obtain by hearing the profound principle and giving rise to faith with a sincere heart?"
The Buddha said, "Listen attentively, Vajrapāṇi! In future ages,
if there are faithful men and women, as well as our fourfold assembly of disciples,
who resolve to copy this sūtra."
This is equivalent to transcribing all the sūtras spoken by nine hundred and ninety billion nayutas of Tathāgatas;
it is equivalent to having planted roots of goodness long ago before those nine hundred and ninety billion nayutas of Tathāgatas.
That is to say, all those Tathāgatas likewise empower and protect him with eyes of affection,
just as a compassionate mother protects her young child.
If a person reads and recites this single fascicle of the sutra,
it is as if they have read and recited the scriptures spoken by all Buddhas of the past, present, and future. Because of this,
[they shall obtain such merit].
Ninety-nine hundred thousand million *koṭi*s of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
arrived in dense succession, filling every space like sesame seeds piled one upon another.
Day and night, they manifest their bodies to empower that person.
In this way, all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas—as numerous as the sands of countless Ganges Rivers—arrive one after another;
before the previous assembly has departed, the subsequent multitude arrives again, shifting and revolving in an instant as they proceed further.
It is like fine sand in a rapidly swirling whirlpool of water,
which cannot remain stationary but turns back and forth;
yet if someone were to offer this sutra incense, flowers, scented unguents, flower garlands, robes, and exquisite ornaments, [the merit would be immeasurable].
Immediately, before those ninety-nine hundred thousand million *koṭi* Tathāgatas of the ten directions,
[he offered] divine incense, flowers, clothing, and ornaments made of the seven precious gems.
Even if one were to pile up offerings as high as Mount Sumeru to provide for them,
the planting of roots of goodness would likewise be of such measure.
At that time, the eight classes of beings— devas, nāgas, and so forth, including humans and non-humans— heard this teaching.
Each harboring a sense of wonder, they said to one another:
"How marvelous! This heap of decayed earth possesses such majestic power;
it is through the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s spiritual authority that such a miraculous transformation has occurred."
Vajrapāṇi again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions has this stūpa made of the seven precious jewels now appeared as a mound of earth?"
The Buddha told Vajrapāṇi:
"This is not a mere heap of earth, but rather a most exquisite and great jeweled stūpa.
It remains hidden and unmanifest because the karmic fruits of sentient beings are inferior."
Because the Tathāgata’s entire body is concealed within the stūpa, it cannot be destroyed.
How could the Tathāgata’s adamantine treasury-body ever be ruined?
After my parinirvāṇa, during the time when the final dharma (mappō) exerts its pressure, [this body shall remain].
If there are sentient beings who practice unrighteousness and should consequently fall into hell,
who do not believe in the Triple Gem and fail to plant roots of goodness—
for these causes and conditions, the Buddha-dharma shall become obscured.
Nevertheless, this stūpa remains firm and indestructible,
sustained by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas;
yet it is obscured by the delusions and hindrances of sentient beings who lack wisdom.
They merely let precious treasures go to waste without knowing how to employ them;
for this reason, I now shed tears,
and those Tathāgatas likewise all shed tears.
Furthermore, the Buddha addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"If there are sentient beings who transcribe this sūtra and place it within a stūpa,
that stūpa shall become a *stūpa* of the Vajragarbha of all Tathāgatas."
It is also a stūpa empowered by the secret heart-mantra of all Tathāgatas;
it is, in fact, a stūpa of nine hundred ninety million billion Tathāgatas.
It is also the stūpa of the uṣṇīṣa and the buddha-eye of all Tathāgatas;
it is protected by the spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas.
If this sūtra is placed within a Buddha image or within a stūpa, [it shall be so].
That image was fashioned from the seven precious jewels; its spiritual efficacy responded to the mind, such that no wish remained unfulfilled.
Its stūpa featured a parasol, a jeweled net, a wheel, a hub, and a dew-dish.
The pillars, bases, foundations, and steps inscribed with the syllable *de* and adorned with bells and chimes shall be prepared according to one's capacity—
whether of earth, wood, stone, or brick—
and through the power of the sutra, they shall spontaneously become the seven precious jewels.
All Tathāgatas empower this sūtra with their majestic power,
sustaining it through their blessing with truthful speech.
If there are sentient beings who [approach] this stūpa...
By prostrating and making offerings of even a single incense stick or a single flower,
the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas will be extinguished all at once;
one shall be spared from calamities and misfortunes in this life and be born into the family of the Buddha after death.
If there are those who are destined to fall into the Avīci Hell,
yet perform even a single prostration before this stūpa, [they shall be liberated].
Or by circumambulating once to the right,
one blocks the gates of hell and opens the path to Bodhi.
At whatever place a stupa or an image is located, [one should perform this].
Protected by the spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas,
that place shall not be harmed by violent winds, thunder, or lightning strikes;
nor shall it be injured by venomous snakes, vipers, poisonous insects, or poisonous beasts.
They shall not be harmed by lions, mad elephants, tigers, wolves, jackals, bees, or wasps;
nor shall they have any fear of yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, nāgas,
piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, kimpuruṣas, apasmāras, or other malevolent spirits.
Furthermore, they shall not be afflicted by any diseases of cold or heat,
nor by scrofula, carbuncles, sores, warts, or leprosy.
If anyone should even briefly behold this stupa, it will be able to eliminate all calamities and misfortunes.
In that place, there shall be no affliction from humans, horses, or six kinds of domestic animals, nor from boys or girls, nor from pestilence.
They shall not meet with untimely death or perish by unnatural means;
they shall not be harmed by swords, staves, water, or fire.
They shall not be invaded by thieves, bandits, or enemies;
nor shall they have the miseries of famine or poverty.
Malevolent enchantments and curses shall find no opportunity to take hold of them.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues, shall guard [them] day and night.
The twenty-eight great yakṣa generals,
the sun, moon, five planets, banners, clouds, and comets shall likewise provide protection and support day and night.
All the dragon kings infuse their vital energy so that rain falls in accordance with the seasons.
All the devas, including those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
descend three times a day to make offerings as well.
All the sages assembled there at the three times of day,
praising him with hymns, circumambulating him, prostrating in gratitude, and gazing up at him in reverence.
Śakra-devānām-indra, together with the celestial maidens, [did likewise].
They descend three times each day and night to make offerings;
that place is then protected and empowered by all Tathāgatas.
Because it contains the sūtra, the stūpa is likewise so.
If a person constructs a stūpa using earth, stone, wood, gold, silver, copper, or lead,
and inscribes this divine mantra within it,
as soon as it has been placed therein—
That stupa was composed of the seven treasures;
its upper and lower tiers, the *āmalaka* bowls, the parasols,
the bells, and the wheel-axles were all made purely of the seven treasures.
On the four sides of that stūpa are the forms of the Tathāgatas;
by virtue of the essential Dharma,
all Tathāgatas remain steadfastly present, guarding and sustaining it day and night without departing.
By the power of the mantra, that wondrous treasure-store of the entire-body relics within the stupa made of the seven precious gems was raised aloft,
reaching as high as the palace of the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
All the devas stand surrounding the stupa, gazing upon it day and night, guarding and making offerings to it.
Vajrapāṇi asked: "By what causes and conditions [is this so]?"
Such are the exceptionally sublime merits of this dharma.
The Buddha said, "You should know that it is due to the majestic spiritual power of this Ratnaketudhāraṇī.
Vajrapāṇi then spoke.
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on us and speak this dhāraṇī. The Buddha said,
"Listen attentively and keep it in mind without forgetting."
The manifested bodies and radiant forms of all Tathāgatas of the present and future,
as well as the entire bodily relics (śarīra) of all Buddhas of the past,
are all contained within the Ratnaketudhāraṇī.
The three bodies of all these Tathāgatas are also contained therein.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this dhāraṇī: *Namaḥ siddhaye dvikāya sarvatathāgate*.
Tadnam oṃ tribhuvi bhava nāvali vajri vajradhe julu julu dhara dhara sarvatathāgata dāstu dhari pātame bhavati jayavari muḥ.

Vara (29) sarvatathāgata (30) yogīśvarī muñce muñce (31) mukti mukti (32) sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhita (33) dattavati svāhā (34).
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ samayādhiṣṭhitāya svāhā. Sarvatathāgatahrīṇaya dhātu-mudrāyai svāhā. Supratiṣṭhe.
Tadastu tathāgatādhiṣṭhite hulu hulu hūṃ hūṃ svāhā. (37) Oṃ sarvatathāgata-uṣṇīṣa-dhātu-mudrāṇi sarvatathāgatam. (38)
*Sadhātu vaimuṣṭi tiṣṭha hūṃ hūṃ svāhā.* (39) At that time,
the Buddha, having spoken this divine mantra, [remained silent].
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, emerged from the midst of the heaps of earth and uttered words of praise, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Śākyamuni World-Honored One!
You have appeared in this world of turbid evil to benefit those sentient beings who are without refuge or protection."
He shall expound the profound Dharma.
Thus, these essential teachings will long abide in the world,
bringing vast benefit, peace, and happiness to many.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
This essential teaching possesses inexhaustible spiritual power and boundless benefit."
It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel atop a banner that constantly rains down precious treasures to fulfill all wishes;
I have now briefly described but one ten-thousandth part of it.
You should remember and uphold this for the benefit of all beings.
If there are wicked people who die and fall into hell,
suffering without interruption and with no hope of escape, [this practice shall deliver them].
If the descendants of such a person recite the aforementioned divine mantra seven times while calling out the deceased’s name,
the molten copper and glowing iron will suddenly transform into a pool of water endowed with the eight meritorious qualities.
A lotus grows from beneath his feet, and a precious canopy rests upon his crown.
The gates of hell break open and the path to Bodhi unfolds;
that lotus flies forth as he arrives in the realm of Sukhāvatī.
The knowledge of all modes naturally manifests;
his eloquence is inexhaustible as he stands in the stage of the position immediately preceding Buddhahood.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, due to the retribution of their grave offenses, [are unable to perceive him].
When a hundred ailments gather in the body and painful afflictions press upon the mind,
recite this divine mantra twenty-one times;
then a hundred ailments and ten thousand vexations will be extinguished all at once.
Their lifespan will be extended and their merit inexhaustible.
Furthermore, if there are those who, due to the karma of stinginess and greed, are born into impoverished families where clothing does not cover their bodies and food does not sustain their lives;
Emaciated, decrepit, and obscured, such a person is loathed and despised by others.
Feeling shame, they enter the mountains to break and gather ownerless, withered flowers;
or they grind rotten wood and use it as incense.
He went before the stūpa to prostrate, make offerings,
circumambulate it seven times, and weep as he repented his transgressions;
this was due to the power of the divine mantra and the majestic virtue of the stūpa.
The retribution of poverty was extinguished and wealth suddenly arrived;
the seven treasures fell like rain, lacking nothing.
At this very time, he further adorned the Buddha-dharma and bestowed gifts upon the poor and destitute.
If there are those who are stingy with their wealth and treasures,
their [merit] will suddenly perish; yet if there are others who, for the sake of planting roots of goodness, construct stupas according to their means—
whether using clay or bricks— according to what they are able to provide.
Make it as large as an *āmra* fruit and about four finger-widths high;
write the divine mantra within it,
and carry it while making offerings of incense and flowers with prostrations.
By the power of that mantra and his faith,
a great cloud of fragrance emerged from within the small stupa;
the scent and the light of the cloud pervaded the entire Dharma-realm.
Fragrant and radiant, they extensively perform the Buddha-work.
The merit thereby obtained is as described above;
to state the essential point: there are no vows that remain unfulfilled.
If there are disciples of the fourfold assembly— sons and daughters of good family— in the final age who,
for the sake of the unsurpassed path, exert all their strength to construct stupas and enshrine this divine mantra,
the merit they shall obtain cannot be fully described.
If a person seeking merit goes to a stūpa and offers a single flower or a single incense stick, performing prostrations, making offerings, and circumambulating clockwise,
through this merit, official rank and glory will arrive spontaneously without being sought.
Longevity and wealth will increase spontaneously without the need for prayer;
enemies and bandits will be defeated naturally without being pursued;
and malicious thoughts or curses will revert to their source without fail.
Pestilence and noxious influences will not arise but will naturally avoid them;
good men and virtuous women will be obtained without seeking;
worthy men and beautiful women will be born without prayer.
All their wishes shall be fulfilled according to their desires.
As for those such as crows, sparrows, owls, hawks,
doves, pigeons, owlets, dogs, wolves, jackals, mosquitoes, gadflies, ants, and termites—
Having briefly come upon the shadow of the stupa and trodden the grass of the practice ground,
one shatters the veils of delusion and awakens to ignorance;
suddenly entering the Buddha’s household, one freely receives the wealth of the Dharma.
How much more so for those among the multitude who see the form of the stupa,
hear the sound of its bells, hear its name, or even fall within its shadow—
their karmic obstructions will all be extinguished, and whatever they seek will be fulfilled as they wish.
One attains peace and security in the present life and rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss hereafter.
Alternatively, a person may, according to their capacity, apply a single lump of clay to the crumbling walls of a stupa,
or move a single fist-sized stone to support a leaning stupa pillar.
By virtue of these merits, one’s blessings will increase and one’s life will be prolonged;
after the end of this life, one will become a wheel-turning monarch.
If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are disciples of the fourfold assembly...
Therefore, before this stupa, in order to deliver beings from the realm of suffering,
one should make offerings of incense and flowers, sincerely make vows, and recite the divine mantra;
with every word and every phrase, it shall emit great radiance.
The light illuminates and touches the instruments of suffering in the three miserable realms, causing them all to vanish;
sentient beings are liberated from suffering, and the sprouts of the Buddha-seed begin to grow.
According to their wishes, they are reborn in the pure lands of the ten directions.
If a person goes to the peak of a high mountain and recites the mantra with a sincere mind,
all worlds— whether far or near— will come within the range of their visual faculty.
In the mountains, valleys, forests, wilds, rivers, lakes, streams, and oceans—
among all the living beings therein, whether feathered, furred, scaly, or shelled—
they shatter the veils of delusion and awaken from ignorance.
The manifestation of the three original Buddha-natures ultimately abides within Great Nirvana.
If one were to travel along the path with such a person, [one would likewise reach that state].
Whether they touch the robe or the wind from it, tread upon its tracks,
merely see his face, or briefly exchange words— with such people as these,
their grave offenses are entirely extinguished and they achieve the perfection of *siddhi*.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"I now entrust this scripture of secret mantras to you all;
you must honor, protect, and maintain it, and cause it to circulate throughout the world."
"Do not allow the transmission of this to sentient beings to be interrupted. Vajrapāṇi said,
"I am now fortunate to have received the World-Honored One’s entrustment."
We only pray that, in order to repay the profound and heavy kindness of the World-Honored One,
we may protect, uphold, disseminate, and proclaim [this teaching] throughout all worlds day and night;
and that if there are sentient beings who copy, receive, uphold, and maintain it in their minds without interruption, [we shall do so for them].
"We shall command Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Great Kings, the nāgas,
and the eight classes of spirits to guard [this person] day and night, never for a moment abandoning them.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, Vajrapāṇi!"
"For the sake of the great benefit of all sentient beings in future ages,
you shall protect and uphold this Dharma so that it is not severed.
At that time, the World-Honored One...
Having performed extensive Buddha-works by reciting this Ratnaketudhāraṇī,
he then went to that brahmin’s house to receive various offerings.
He caused the people and devas of that time to obtain great benefit and merit, and then returned to his own dwelling.
At that time, the great assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen;
devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth—[were present].
All were filled with great joy, believed, accepted, and practiced it.
This sutra is contained within the eighth volume of the *Daming Zang* (Great Bright Treasury),
in the section on Ritual Procedures (*vidhi*).
This is the same text as the *Ratnaketuparivarta-dhāraṇī-sūtra* translated by Amoghavajra;
however, there are not a few differences between them.
As for this version:
It was requested by the three masters Bianzhao Jingang, Cijue, and Zhizheng;
its phrasing and meaning are fluent and clear.
Previously, the Venerable Liangtai annotated this text, and it has circulated throughout the world.
Now, in connection with the carving of these various manuals,
I have further noted the differences between the editions in the Tripiṭaka and those on the covers;
the former are made of wood.
Abbot of Fǎngshān, Qīnxī Kuàidào, records this for Cishùn.
